PRINCIPLES.name: Efficiency
PRINCIPLES.def: The institution resolves disputes while minimizing resource use and maximizing net benefit, tempered by the complexity of the case.

PRINCIPLES.name: Speediness
PRINCIPLES.def: Dispute resolution without undue delay, through swift, streamlined and unbureaucratic procedures.

PRINCIPLES.name: Accountability
PRINCIPLES.def: The institution promotes transparency and has mechanisms making it, and its practitioners, answerable to society for performance.

PRINCIPLES.name: Accessibility
PRINCIPLES.def: The institution takes measures to reduce or remove barriers to resolving disputes — including factors that quietly put users off.

PRINCIPLES.name: Independence
PRINCIPLES.def: The institution performs its functions by reference to the law and merit, without inappropriate external influence.

PRINCIPLES.name: Impartiality
PRINCIPLES.def: The institution guards against actual or perceived bias, including through a culture of declaring and managing conflicts of interest.

PRINCIPLES.name: Fairness
PRINCIPLES.def: Outcomes are not only fair but are reached, and seen to be reached, in a fair way.

PRINCIPLES.name: Equality
PRINCIPLES.def: The institution provides for equality by facilitating fair and equitable redress for disputes.

PRINCIPLES.name: Professionalism
PRINCIPLES.def: The institution has specialized expertise, recruits on merit, trains its people, and holds them to published standards of conduct.

PRINCIPLES.name: Enforcement
PRINCIPLES.def: The institution has mechanisms to ensure effective compliance with the final resolution.

PRINCIPLES.name: Voluntarism
PRINCIPLES.def: Parties have a free choice of method and retain control over the process and its outcome. Not absolute: law or a collective agreement may prescribe.

PRINCIPLES.name: Confidentiality
PRINCIPLES.def: Nothing produced in the dispute resolution process is disclosed to non-participants, subject to specified exceptions.

PRINCIPLES.name: Prevention
PRINCIPLES.def: An effective institution assists in preventing disputes, not only in resolving them once they have erupted.

SYMPTOMS.text: The only office that accepts filings is 400 kilometres away, and it opens 09:00 to 15:00 on weekdays.
SYMPTOMS.why: Opening hours that require a day off, and a journey most claimants cannot afford, are exactly the barriers the tool means by factors that “obstruct or disincentivize use”.

SYMPTOMS.text: The hearing is adjourned because nobody can find the case file. It is the second time this year.
SYMPTOMS.why: Case management and accurate, retrievable records sit under efficiency. Every lost file is a wasted hearing day paid for by both parties.

SYMPTOMS.text: The law sets a 30-day limit for conciliation. Last year the average was eleven months. Nobody reports that figure.
SYMPTOMS.why: Speediness is measured by whether statutory deadlines are met and whether delay is monitored at all. Unmeasured delay is nobody’s problem.

SYMPTOMS.text: You ask how many cases the institution closed last year. Nobody can tell you, and nothing is published.
SYMPTOMS.why: Public performance reporting is the cheapest accountability measure there is, and its absence is the easiest finding to act on.

SYMPTOMS.text: The institution’s budget was cut by 40 per cent the year after it ruled against a state-owned enterprise.
SYMPTOMS.why: Funding is the quietest lever of all. If the budget can be squeezed after an unpopular decision, the institution is not independent whatever the statute says.

SYMPTOMS.text: The arbitrator’s brother-in-law is HR director at the respondent company. He did not mention it.
SYMPTOMS.why: Independence is about the institution and the outside world; impartiality is about this individual and this case. The failure here is the undeclared interest.

SYMPTOMS.text: The decision arrives as a single line: “Claim dismissed.” No reasons are given.
SYMPTOMS.why: Reasoned decision-making is a fairness element. Justice has to be seen to be done, and an unexplained outcome cannot be.

SYMPTOMS.text: Women are 42 per cent of the workforce and 9 per cent of claimants. Nobody has asked why.
SYMPTOMS.why: Equality is not about who walks through the door. It is about who never does — which is why the tool asks for disaggregated data.

SYMPTOMS.text: The conciliator transferred in from the vehicle licensing desk three weeks ago, after two days of induction.
SYMPTOMS.why: Conciliation is a taught, accredited skill that decays without practice. Specialization and induction are both professionalism elements.

SYMPTOMS.text: The tribunal awarded three months’ pay. Eighteen months later the worker is still trying to collect it.
SYMPTOMS.why: An unenforceable award is an expensive piece of paper. A system can score well on everything else and still fail here.

SYMPTOMS.text: Both parties want to attempt a settlement they design themselves. They are told the matter must go to arbitration, but no legal or agreed requirement is identified.
SYMPTOMS.why: Voluntarism means free choice of method and control of the outcome. It is not absolute — but a blanket requirement with no justification is a failure.

SYMPTOMS.text: What a party said in mediation last month appears in the employer’s submission to the court.
SYMPTOMS.why: No confidentiality, no candour. No candour, no settlement. Exceptions have to be defined in advance, not improvised.

SYMPTOMS.text: The same shift-pattern dispute has arrived from the same sector eleven times. Nobody has asked why.
SYMPTOMS.why: Repeated disputes with the same underlying cause call for analysis and preventive action, rather than processing every case in isolation.

SYMPTOMS.text: The filing form runs to nine pages and must be countersigned by an advocate.
SYMPTOMS.why: A procedure only a lawyer can start is a procedure most workers cannot use. Complexity is a barrier like any other.

SYMPTOMS.text: Appointments to the tribunal are made personally by the minister. There are no published criteria.
SYMPTOMS.why: Transparent, merit-based appointment is an independence element. An appointment that is a gift can be withdrawn like one.

SYMPTOMS.text: A conciliator accepts a lunch invitation from one party’s lawyer while the case is live.
SYMPTOMS.why: The standard covers perceived as well as actual bias. Nothing improper need have been said for the process to look bought.

SYMPTOMS.text: A settlement signed at conciliation cannot be enforced without starting fresh proceedings in another court.
SYMPTOMS.why: Enforcement includes an accessible way to give settlements legal effect and secure compliance. Ratification may be required in some systems; unnecessary fresh litigation can undermine the remedy.

SYMPTOMS.text: A case has lain dormant for fourteen months. There is no route to complain about the delay.
SYMPTOMS.why: Both are defensible. Speediness asks whether delay is monitored and whether there is a complaints route; accountability asks whether anyone answers for performance. Plenty of systems are slow — the ones that improve are the ones you can complain to.

CARDS.name: Standing joint forum
CARDS.desc: A regular body where management and workers discuss operational matters that are not on the bargaining table.

CARDS.name: Notice and consultation
CARDS.desc: Tell people before you change something that affects them, and hear them before it is final.

CARDS.name: Written grievance procedure
CARDS.desc: A route anyone can find and use, uncomplicated, with formality kept to a minimum.

CARDS.name: Time limits, measured
CARDS.desc: A deadline at each stage, compliance reported monthly to someone senior.

CARDS.name: Right to representation
CARDS.desc: Enable representation and accompaniment through the applicable grievance procedure, including appropriate workers’ representatives.

CARDS.name: Supervisor conflict training
CARDS.desc: Line managers equipped to handle a disagreement rather than escalate it.

CARDS.name: A second door
CARDS.desc: Another way in besides the line manager, and people know it exists.

CARDS.name: Internal mediation
CARDS.desc: A neutral inside the organization that both sides actually trust.

CARDS.name: The CBA disputes procedure
CARDS.desc: Use the dispute procedure agreed in the collective agreement, while preserving applicable legal rights and remedies.

CARDS.name: External conciliation
CARDS.desc: Invite an external conciliator to help the parties find a voluntary settlement. Check applicable procedures and limitation periods.

CARDS.name: Restate the decision
CARDS.desc: Put the original decision in writing, formally, and hold the line.

SCENARIOS.name: The Roster
SCENARIOS.blurb: An operational change nobody explained. Five stages from a shrug to a strike notice.
SCENARIOS.fail: Notice of strike is served. The dispute is now public, expensive and out of your hands.

stages.text: A supervisor rewrites next month’s shift roster. No explanation is given. Two workers object at the end of the shift.

c1.msg: The roster change goes to the joint forum first. Both objections surface there and are settled before anyone feels ambushed.

c2.msg: You explain the reason and hear the objection before the roster is final. It takes nine minutes and the dispute never exists.

c3.msg: A procedure exists, and they could use it. They have not yet, and the roster still makes no sense to them.

c4.msg: The immediate issue is the unexplained roster change and the two workers’ objections. A deadline accelerates a process; it cannot by itself correct its substance, independence or representation. In this round it remains unanswered, so the dispute advances.

c5.msg: The immediate issue is the unexplained roster change and the two workers’ objections. Representation supports a fair process, but does not by itself answer the complaint or require the other side to agree. In this round it remains unanswered, so the dispute advances.

c6.msg: The supervisor is trained for exactly this. She explains the reasoning, takes the objection seriously, and adjusts one shift.

c7.msg: They now have somewhere else to raise it — useful, but the original grievance is still unanswered.

c8.msg: The immediate issue is the unexplained roster change and the two workers’ objections. A mediator needs both parties’ agreement and a live issue they are willing to address; an offer alone does not settle the case. In this round it remains unanswered, so the dispute advances.

c9.msg: The immediate issue is the unexplained roster change and the two workers’ objections. An agreed collective procedure must apply to this issue and be activated by the parties; citing it alone is insufficient. In this round it remains unanswered, so the dispute advances.

c10.msg: You have called in the public conciliator over a roster query. It signals that this is already a dispute, and now it is one.

c11.msg: You put the roster in writing and restate it. It reads as a refusal to engage, and the shift closes ranks.

stages.text: The supervisor tells them the decision is final. They repeat the conversation to the rest of the shift over lunch.

c1.msg: The immediate issue is the supervisor’s refusal to reconsider and the shift’s growing distrust. A standing forum can support prevention and consultation, but a meeting alone does not determine this complaint. In this round it remains unanswered, so the dispute advances.

c2.msg: Consultation after the decision is final is not consultation, and they say so.

c3.msg: You point them at the grievance procedure. Correct, but it reads as being sent away, and the shift is still talking.

c4.msg: The immediate issue is the supervisor’s refusal to reconsider and the shift’s growing distrust. A deadline accelerates a process; it cannot by itself correct its substance, independence or representation. In this round it remains unanswered, so the dispute advances.

c5.msg: They are told they may bring a representative. Helpful, and it also confirms to them that this is now formal.

c6.msg: The supervisor reopens it herself rather than defending the position. The shift sees someone listening, and it stops there.

c7.msg: They raise it through the second door. Someone outside the reporting line looks at it on its merits and fixes the roster.

c8.msg: An internal mediator takes thirty minutes with the supervisor and the two workers. Everyone leaves having been heard.

c9.msg: The immediate issue is the supervisor’s refusal to reconsider and the shift’s growing distrust. An agreed collective procedure must apply to this issue and be activated by the parties; citing it alone is insufficient. In this round it remains unanswered, so the dispute advances.

c10.msg: The immediate issue is the supervisor’s refusal to reconsider and the shift’s growing distrust. External conciliation needs the parties’ engagement and a defined dispute; referring out does not itself answer the underlying concern. In this round it remains unanswered, so the dispute advances.

c11.msg: A second written restatement. The shift now has evidence that nobody will move, and the rep is brought in.

stages.text: The union representative emails HR setting out the objection. Nine days pass with no reply.

c1.msg: The joint forum is the right machinery at the wrong moment. This is past prevention.

c2.msg: The immediate issue is the unanswered representative’s email after nine days. Information and consultation must be meaningful and directed to the disputed issue; merely announcing the decision does not review it. In this round it remains unanswered, so the dispute advances.

c3.msg: You activate the grievance procedure, arrange a prompt meeting with the representative and address the roster objection. In this case the parties agree a workable change.

c4.msg: The clock is the whole problem. A measured deadline means the email is answered on day two and the heat goes out of it.

c5.msg: Representation is confirmed. The rep is already involved, so this changes little.

c6.msg: The immediate issue is the unanswered representative’s email after nine days. Training helps managers handle future conflict; it does not by itself supply the missing review or agreement in this case. In this round it remains unanswered, so the dispute advances.

c7.msg: Another entry point helps future cases. It does not answer the email sitting in the inbox.

c8.msg: Mediation is offered and taken. Nine days of silence is undone by one scheduled conversation.

c9.msg: The immediate issue is the unanswered representative’s email after nine days. An agreed collective procedure must apply to this issue and be activated by the parties; citing it alone is insufficient. In this round it remains unanswered, so the dispute advances.

c10.msg: The immediate issue is the unanswered representative’s email after nine days. External conciliation needs the parties’ engagement and a defined dispute; referring out does not itself answer the underlying concern. In this round it remains unanswered, so the dispute advances.

c11.msg: You reply after nine days by restating the decision. The delay and the content both land badly.

stages.text: A formal grievance is filed. HR acknowledges receipt and schedules nothing.

c1.msg: The immediate issue is the formal grievance with no hearing scheduled. A standing forum can support prevention and consultation, but a meeting alone does not determine this complaint. In this round it remains unanswered, so the dispute advances.

c2.msg: The immediate issue is the formal grievance with no hearing scheduled. Information and consultation must be meaningful and directed to the disputed issue; merely announcing the decision does not review it. In this round it remains unanswered, so the dispute advances.

c3.msg: The procedure exists and is now in use. It is still not moving.

c4.msg: Measured deadlines trigger a prompt hearing rather than another acknowledgement. The roster concern is heard and the parties agree a workable response.

c5.msg: The worker and representative take part in a properly convened hearing. The concern is tested, reasons are given and a practical shift arrangement is accepted in this case.

c6.msg: Training the supervisor is the right fix three weeks too late.

c7.msg: The immediate issue is the formal grievance with no hearing scheduled. Another entry point needs someone empowered to act; signposting alone leaves the substantive issue unresolved. In this round it remains unanswered, so the dispute advances.

c8.msg: Mediation runs alongside the grievance and produces an agreed shift swap. The grievance is withdrawn.

c9.msg: The collective agreement route is available. Nobody has opened it yet.

c10.msg: The immediate issue is the formal grievance with no hearing scheduled. External conciliation needs the parties’ engagement and a defined dispute; referring out does not itself answer the underlying concern. In this round it remains unanswered, so the dispute advances.

c11.msg: Restating the decision in response to a formal grievance is a procedural failure, and the union now has a case worth running.

c9.msg: The parties activate the dispute procedure in their collective agreement and reach an agreement within its timetable. Applicable statutory rights remain available.

SCENARIOS.name: The Dismissal
SCENARIOS.blurb: An individual case handled at speed. Five stages from a ten-minute meeting to a tribunal claim.
SCENARIOS.fail: The claim proceeds to a tribunal hearing. Costs and management time rise, and the tribunal will determine the merits. Going to court is a legitimate route, not evidence that the claimant was wrong.

stages.text: A storekeeper is dismissed for alleged theft after a ten-minute meeting with her supervisor. She denies it.

c1.msg: The immediate issue is the dismissal imposed without a meaningful opportunity to answer. A standing forum can support prevention and consultation, but a meeting alone does not determine this complaint. In this round it remains unanswered, so the dispute advances.

c2.msg: The immediate issue is the dismissal imposed without a meaningful opportunity to answer. Information and consultation must be meaningful and directed to the disputed issue; merely announcing the decision does not review it. In this round it remains unanswered, so the dispute advances.

c3.msg: You reopen the dismissal through an appropriate review: disclose the allegation, hear the worker’s response and examine the evidence. A reasoned correction of the decision settles this fictional case.

c4.msg: The immediate issue is the dismissal imposed without a meaningful opportunity to answer. A deadline accelerates a process; it cannot by itself correct its substance, independence or representation. In this round it remains unanswered, so the dispute advances.

c5.msg: You permit appropriate representation and reopen the dismissal for a fair review. The evidence is tested and a reasoned outcome is accepted in this case; representation alone would not guarantee that result.

c6.msg: Better-trained supervisors would have prevented this. It has already happened.

c7.msg: She has somewhere else to take it. The dismissal still happened after a ten-minute meeting.

c8.msg: The immediate issue is the dismissal imposed without a meaningful opportunity to answer. A mediator needs both parties’ agreement and a live issue they are willing to address; an offer alone does not settle the case. In this round it remains unanswered, so the dispute advances.

c9.msg: The immediate issue is the dismissal imposed without a meaningful opportunity to answer. An agreed collective procedure must apply to this issue and be activated by the parties; citing it alone is insufficient. In this round it remains unanswered, so the dispute advances.

c10.msg: In this fictional case, referring out without offering a meaningful internal review leaves the hearing complaint unanswered. External conciliation can be appropriate early by agreement; it does not cure this omission by itself.

c11.msg: Confirming the dismissal in writing without a hearing is the single most expensive thing you can do here.

stages.text: She asks to appeal. She is told she may bring a colleague, but not her union representative.

c1.msg: The immediate issue is the blanket restriction on the worker’s chosen union representative. A standing forum can support prevention and consultation, but a meeting alone does not determine this complaint. In this round it remains unanswered, so the dispute advances.

c2.msg: The immediate issue is the blanket restriction on the worker’s chosen union representative. Information and consultation must be meaningful and directed to the disputed issue; merely announcing the decision does not review it. In this round it remains unanswered, so the dispute advances.

c3.msg: The procedure is applied as written, including the representation clause everyone had forgotten.

c4.msg: The immediate issue is the blanket restriction on the worker’s chosen union representative. A deadline accelerates a process; it cannot by itself correct its substance, independence or representation. In this round it remains unanswered, so the dispute advances.

c5.msg: You remove the blanket restriction and enable appropriate representation under the applicable procedure. The appeal is heard fairly and the parties resolve the case.

c6.msg: The immediate issue is the blanket restriction on the worker’s chosen union representative. Training helps managers handle future conflict; it does not by itself supply the missing review or agreement in this case. In this round it remains unanswered, so the dispute advances.

c7.msg: An alternative route is offered. The representation problem is still there.

c8.msg: Mediation is offered and she is willing. The appeal question remains unresolved.

c9.msg: The immediate issue is the blanket restriction on the worker’s chosen union representative. An agreed collective procedure must apply to this issue and be activated by the parties; citing it alone is insufficient. In this round it remains unanswered, so the dispute advances.

c10.msg: The immediate issue is the blanket restriction on the worker’s chosen union representative. External conciliation needs the parties’ engagement and a defined dispute; referring out does not itself answer the underlying concern. In this round it remains unanswered, so the dispute advances.

c11.msg: You restate the restriction. You have now created a second, cleaner complaint on top of the first.

stages.text: The appeal is heard by the same manager who took the decision to dismiss.

c1.msg: A joint forum has no role in an individual disciplinary appeal.

c2.msg: The immediate issue is the original manager hearing the appeal against their own decision. Information and consultation must be meaningful and directed to the disputed issue; merely announcing the decision does not review it. In this round it remains unanswered, so the dispute advances.

c3.msg: The immediate issue is the original manager hearing the appeal against their own decision. A procedure needs an actual hearing, a responsible decision-maker and follow-through, rather than a form on its own. In this round it remains unanswered, so the dispute advances.

c4.msg: The appeal happens quickly. Speed does not cure who is sitting in the chair.

c5.msg: She is properly represented at the appeal. It is still the same manager deciding.

c6.msg: The immediate issue is the original manager hearing the appeal against their own decision. Training helps managers handle future conflict; it does not by itself supply the missing review or agreement in this case. In this round it remains unanswered, so the dispute advances.

c7.msg: A different route means a different decision-maker. Someone with no stake in the original decision hears it.

c8.msg: Both parties accept a neutral mediator who had no role in the dismissal. They agree a settlement, without treating mediation as a substitute for an independent appeal if no settlement is reached.

c9.msg: The immediate issue is the original manager hearing the appeal against their own decision. An agreed collective procedure must apply to this issue and be activated by the parties; citing it alone is insufficient. In this round it remains unanswered, so the dispute advances.

c10.msg: The immediate issue is the original manager hearing the appeal against their own decision. External conciliation needs the parties’ engagement and a defined dispute; referring out does not itself answer the underlying concern. In this round it remains unanswered, so the dispute advances.

c11.msg: The same manager confirms his own decision, in writing. There is now nothing left to argue about internally.

SCENARIOS.name: The Restructure
SCENARIOS.blurb: Sixty jobs and a plan nobody has announced. Five stages from a boardroom decision to a go-slow.
SCENARIOS.fail: The go-slow spreads to two more sites. Output is down, the press has the story, and the restructure has stalled.

stages.text: Head office decides to outsource the warehouse. Sixty jobs are affected. Nothing has been announced.

c1.msg: The joint forum opens an early discussion about the proposed outsourcing. The parties identify concerns and agree consultation and bargaining arrangements without replacing any collective bargaining rights.

c2.msg: You tell the workforce and their representatives before the decision is irreversible, and you hear them. It changes two things in the plan and most of the anger never forms.

c3.msg: In this case, directing the whole workforce to individual grievances leaves the collective outsourcing proposal unexplained. Grievance procedures can cover joint rights complaints, but are not a substitute for bargaining over proposed terms.

c4.msg: The immediate issue is the unannounced outsourcing proposal affecting sixty jobs. A deadline accelerates a process; it cannot by itself correct its substance, independence or representation. In this round it remains unanswered, so the dispute advances.

c5.msg: The immediate issue is the unannounced outsourcing proposal affecting sixty jobs. Representation supports a fair process, but does not by itself answer the complaint or require the other side to agree. In this round it remains unanswered, so the dispute advances.

c6.msg: The immediate issue is the unannounced outsourcing proposal affecting sixty jobs. Training helps managers handle future conflict; it does not by itself supply the missing review or agreement in this case. In this round it remains unanswered, so the dispute advances.

c8.msg: The immediate issue is the unannounced outsourcing proposal affecting sixty jobs. A mediator needs both parties’ agreement and a live issue they are willing to address; an offer alone does not settle the case. In this round it remains unanswered, so the dispute advances.

c10.msg: Calling the conciliator before announcing anything tells the union there is something to hide.
